blurb: Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens, the data that goes in, and the laws that predict the result.

cards.title: The simplest objective that works

steps.p: Pretraining shows the model text and asks it to predict each next token, over trillions of tokens.
The "right answer" is just the next token in the data, so no human labeling is needed. This is called self-supervised learning.
To predict well, the model has to learn grammar, facts, styles and some reasoning, because all of these make text more predictable.

cards.aside: Predicting the next line of a proof well requires something like understanding the proof.

options: The model grades its own answers
The training targets come from the data itself
cards.why: The data is its own label. Every position in a document gives a free training example: the context so far, and the token that actually follows.

cards.statement: Most pretraining data is labeled by hand.
cards.why: False. It is overwhelmingly raw text — web pages, books, code, papers — filtered automatically. Human-written data matters much more in post-training.

cards.q: Common Crawl, a major source of pretraining text, is…
options: A free archive of billions of web pages collected since 2008
cards.why: An open web archive. It is petabytes of raw crawled pages. Labs filter it heavily — removing duplicates, spam and low-quality text — before training on a small fraction.

cards.title: Meta's Llama 3 models were pretrained on over 15 trillion tokens.
cards.detail: That is roughly 11 trillion words — far more than any human could read in thousands of lifetimes, and about seven times the data used for Llama 2.

cards.statement: A base model, straight out of pretraining, reliably follows instructions like a chatbot.
cards.why: False. A base model continues text. Ask it a question and it may answer — or generate a list of similar questions. Instruction-following comes from post-training.

cards.title: What goes into the mix

steps.p: Near-duplicate pages are removed and classifiers score quality, keeping text that resembles high-quality references.
Labs tune the share of web text, code, math, books and other languages. Mixtures strongly affect what the model is good at.
Text overlapping with evaluation benchmarks is removed, so test scores reflect ability rather than memorization.

cards.aside: Many researchers now argue data curation matters as much as architecture.

cards.q: Why do labs aggressively deduplicate training data?
options: Repeated text wastes compute and encourages verbatim memorization
cards.why: Waste and memorization. Seeing the same passage hundreds of times teaches little new and makes the model more likely to regurgitate it word for word.

cards.statement: Training for several passes over the same data is always as good as training on fresh data.
cards.why: False. Research (Muennighoff et al., 2023) found a few epochs are nearly as good as new data, but returns drop sharply after that. Repeated data is worth less each pass.

options: Models trained repeatedly on their own outputs losing diversity and the rare tails of the data
cards.why: Recursive degradation. A 2024 Nature paper showed that training each generation on the previous generation's output narrows the distribution. Mixing in real data counteracts it.

cards.title: Microsoft's Phi models showed that small models trained on carefully made "textbook-quality" data can outperform much bigger ones.
cards.detail: The 2023 paper "Textbooks Are All You Need" trained a 1.3B-parameter coding model largely on filtered and synthetic educational text, rivaling models many times its size.

options: The stock of high-quality human text running out relative to what scaling demands
cards.why: Running out of good text. Estimates such as Epoch AI's suggest frontier training could use up the stock of public human-written text around the late 2020s, pushing labs toward synthetic data and other modalities.

cards.title: Predictable improvement

steps.p: In 2020, OpenAI researchers found loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute — smoothly, over many orders of magnitude.
Plot loss against compute on log-log axes and you get a nearly straight line. Extending it predicts bigger models.
Labs fit these curves on cheap small runs before spending tens of millions of dollars on a large one.

cards.aside: Loss is predictable; which specific skills appear at a given loss is much less so.

cards.q: A power law relationship, plotted on log-log axes, looks like…
cards.why: A straight line. If y = a·xᵇ, then log y = log a + b·log x. The slope b is the scaling exponent.

cards.statement: OpenAI predicted GPT-4's final loss in advance from much smaller training runs.
cards.why: True. The GPT-4 technical report says its final loss was predicted from models trained with up to 10,000× less compute, using fitted scaling laws.

cards.q: Using Chinchilla's rule of thumb of about 20 tokens per parameter, a compute-optimal 10B model should train on about…
cards.why: About 200 billion. 10 billion × 20. This balances parameters and data for the best loss at a fixed training budget.

cards.statement: Modern small open models are often trained far past the Chinchilla-optimal amount of data.
cards.why: True. Llama 3 8B saw about 15 trillion tokens — nearly 2,000 per parameter. Extra training costs once; a smaller, better model saves money on every query served.

cards.title: Whether abilities "emerge" suddenly with scale is still debated.
cards.detail: Some skills seem to jump from near zero to good at a certain size. A 2023 paper argued much of this is an artifact of all-or-nothing metrics; measured smoothly, improvement often looks gradual.

cards.title: Months on thousands of GPUs

steps.p: The learning rate ramps up over the first steps, then slowly decreases, often along a cosine curve.
Loss sometimes jumps suddenly. Teams roll back to an earlier checkpoint and skip or reorder the offending data.
With tens of thousands of GPUs, something breaks every few hours. Frequent checkpoints and automatic restarts are essential.

cards.aside: Big training runs are as much an operations challenge as a research one.

cards.q: Why do training runs start with a learning-rate warmup?
options: Early updates on random weights are large and unstable, and Adam's statistics aren't settled yet
cards.why: Stability. At the start, gradients are erratic and the optimizer's running averages are empty. Small steps at first prevent an early blow-up.

cards.title: Meta's 54-day Llama 3 405B run hit hundreds of unexpected interruptions.
cards.detail: Its paper reports over 400 unplanned interruptions on a cluster of about 16,000 H100s, most caused by hardware — faulty GPUs and their HBM memory being the leading causes.

cards.q: Large training runs typically achieve what fraction of the GPUs' theoretical peak FLOPs ("MFU")?
cards.why: Roughly 35–45%. Llama 3 reported about 38–43%. Communication, memory traffic and pipeline bubbles eat the rest.

cards.statement: Loss spikes during training are always caused by bad data.
cards.why: False. Optimizer instabilities, numerical issues and learning rates can also cause them. Fixes include rolling back, lowering the learning rate, or architectural tweaks like QK-normalization.

cards.q: Using 6 × parameters × tokens, GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens) needed roughly how much training compute?
cards.why: About 3.1 × 10²³. 6 × 1.75×10¹¹ × 3×10¹¹. The GPT-3 paper reported 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs — the rule of thumb is that accurate.
